title: Justice, excellence, giving to kin
hookLine: Allah commands justice, excellence and giving to kin (16:90), recited in many Friday sermons

lines: THE END OF THE FRIDAY SERMON.
THE SAME LINES, WEEK AFTER WEEK.
cards: If you've ever sat through a Friday prayer in a mosque, you may have heard this verse without knowing its number.
In mosques from Cairo to Chicago, imams often close the second half of the sermon with it, just before the call to stand for prayer. Week after week, the same few lines.
A tradition says the custom goes back to the Umayyad ruler Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz. Whatever the sermon was about, the week ends on these words.

teach.b: Pickthall translates it: "Lo! Allah enjoineth justice and kindness, and giving to kinsfolk, and forbiddeth lewdness and abomination and wickedness. He exhorteth you in order that ye may take heed."
Three things commanded, three forbidden. First commanded: 'adl, justice.
The root carries the sense of balance, of making two sides level, the way a scale settles. Justice is giving each person what is due to them, no more and no less, including the people you don't like.

teach.h: IHSAN: AS IF YOU SEE HIM.
teach.b: Second, ihsan. Pickthall says kindness; others say excellence, or doing what is beautiful.
In a well-known hadith, the angel Jibril asks the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ what ihsan is, and he answers: to worship God as though you see Him, and if you don't see Him, He sees you.
So ihsan is justice with something added: doing more than what's owed, and doing it well. Third, giving to kin.

Not giving in general, though the Qur'an asks for that too: giving to the near ones, the relatives. Notice the order: the scale, then the extra, then the people closest to you, who are often the hardest to be fair to.
A saying attributed to the companion Ibn Mas'ud calls this the most comprehensive verse in the Qur'an for good and for evil.
And a hadith in Tirmidhi says charity to a relative counts twice: once as charity, once as keeping the family tie.

Then the three forbidden: shameful acts; munkar, what is known to be wrong; and baghy, overstepping against others. The verse closes not with a threat but with a reason: He counsels you, so that you might remember.

how: In many mosques the imam recites 16:90 at the end of the Friday sermon before the prayer begins; Muslims cite it as a summary of social ethics and give charity to relatives as both charity and keeping family ties.

o: 'adl: giving each their due, level as a scale
treating everyone exactly alike, whatever they need
punishing wrongdoers as harshly as possible

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: worship as though you see Him

s: 16:90 is often recited at the end of the Friday sermon
in many mosques the imam closes the sermon with it; a tradition traces the custom to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz.
the verse only forbids; it commands nothing
it commands three things, justice, ihsan and giving to kin, before it forbids three.
charity to a relative counts as charity only
a hadith in Tirmidhi says it counts twice: charity, and keeping the family tie.

games.q: the angel Jibril asks the Prophet what ihsan is. what does he answer?
o: worshiping God as though you see Him; and if you don't, He sees you.
games.why: as though you see Him, and if you don't see Him, He sees you. ihsan is doing a thing well because of who's watching.

practice: Picture your family, the whole loose circle of it, parents, siblings, cousins, an aunt you haven't called in a year, and let one face come forward.
What could you give them: money if they need it, or time, a meal, a message, a fair hearing in an old argument? If you pray, ask for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Justice. 'Adl, the level scale, first of three things the verse commands, followed by excellence and giving to kin. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: justice and excellence, the first two things commanded in 16:90.

carryVoice: Your line: justice, excellence, kin. The scale, the extra, the near ones. See you tomorrow.
